en: retrial; re-examination; re-evaluation (of a case or decision)

examples.en: A retrial for that case will be held next year.

examples.ko: 결과에 불만이 있으면 재심을 신청할 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you are unhappy with the result, you can apply for a review.
The judge accepted the request for a retrial.

examples.ko: 재심 결과는 한 달 뒤에 나와요.
examples.en: The result of the re-examination comes out in a month.
The school explained the grade review system.
Some people were found not guilty at a retrial.

explain: 재심은 이미 끝난 재판이나 심사를 다시 하는 거예요. 뉴스와 서류에서 주로 쓰고, 보통 '재심을 청구하다', '재심이 열리다'처럼 말해요. 일상에서 '다시 살펴보다'라고 할 때는 '재검토'가 더 자연스러워요.
explain_en: 재심 is a formal word for redoing a trial or an official review that has already finished. You mostly meet it in news and documents, in phrases like 재심을 청구하다 (file for a retrial). In daily talk, 재검토 (to look over again) sounds more natural.

en: once again; for a second time (formal)

examples.en: The teacher told us to check once more.
The company expressed its apology once again.

examples.ko: 그 사람에게 재차 물어봤지만 대답이 없었어요.
examples.en: I asked that person a second time, but there was no answer.

examples.ko: 점원이 재차 같은 질문을 해서 조금 당황했어요.
examples.en: The clerk asked the same question again, and I was a bit flustered.
The boss stressed it again.
He tried again but failed once more.

explain: 재차는 이미 한 일을 두 번째로 또 한다는 느낌의 말이에요. 말보다 글이나 뉴스, 공식적인 말투에서 많이 써요. 친구와 이야기할 때는 '또', '다시'가 훨씬 자연스러워요.
explain_en: 재차 means doing something a second time, after it was already done once. It fits writing, news and formal speech. With friends, Koreans say 또 or 다시 instead.

en: change of direction, stance or field (e.g. switching sports or beliefs)

examples.ko: 그 선수는 야구에서 축구로 전향을 결심했어요.
examples.en: That athlete decided to switch from baseball to soccer.
Everyone was surprised by the sudden change of course.
Even after the switch, they keep practicing hard.
The coach allowed the player to switch positions.
A reporter asked why they had made the switch.
Changing course is not an easy decision.

explain: 전향은 지금까지 하던 방향이나 입장을 다른 쪽으로 바꾸는 거예요. 스포츠에서는 종목이나 포지션을 바꿀 때, 뉴스에서는 생각이나 입장을 바꿀 때 주로 써요. 일상에서 단순히 마음을 바꿀 때는 '마음이 바뀌다'를 써요.
explain_en: 전향 is a shift away from the direction or stance one held before. In sports it means changing events or positions; in the news it means changing views. For simply changing your mind in daily life, say 마음이 바뀌다.

en: switch; change (one's stance, direction or field)

examples.en: That singer is switching to acting.

examples.ko: 저는 대학 때 수영에서 달리기로 전향했어요.
examples.en: In college I switched from swimming to running.
Next year I will switch to being a director.
The players who switched sports do surprisingly well.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 입장을 바꿔 새 정책 쪽으로 전향했어요.
examples.en: That person changed their position and moved over to the new policy.
After switching to being a chef, I became much happier.

explain: '전향하다'는 하던 일이나 종목을 다른 쪽으로 옮길 때 써요. 직업이 바뀔 때는 '직업을 바꾸다'도 가능하지만, 전향하다는 같은 분야 안에서 방향을 틀 때 더 잘 어울려요. 주로 '~로 전향하다'로 말해요.
explain_en: 전향하다 is used when someone moves from one field, sport or stance to another, usually in the pattern ~로 전향하다. It suits a change of direction within a similar area; for a plain job change, 직업을 바꾸다 also works.

examples.en: We learned about imperialism in history class.

examples.ko: 제국주의 시대에는 많은 나라가 식민지가 되었어요.
examples.en: In the age of imperialism, many countries became colonies.

examples.ko: 그 책은 제국주의의 역사를 쉽게 설명해요.
examples.en: That book explains the history of imperialism in an easy way.
Even after imperialism ended, conflicts remained.

examples.ko: 영화는 제국주의 시대의 아픔을 보여 줘요.
examples.en: The movie shows the pain of the imperialist era.

examples.ko: 선생님은 제국주의가 왜 생겼는지 자세히 설명하셨어요.
examples.en: The teacher explained in detail why imperialism arose.

explain: 제국주의는 힘이 센 나라가 다른 나라나 땅을 차지하려는 생각과 정책이에요. 한국에서는 일제강점기와 연결해서 자주 나오는 말이라서, 역사나 뉴스에서 아주 무겁게 들려요. 보통 '제국주의 시대', '제국주의 국가'처럼 써요.
explain_en: 제국주의 is the policy of a powerful country taking over other lands. In Korea it comes up constantly with the Japanese colonial period, so it carries a heavy tone in history and news. Typical forms are 제국주의 시대 and 제국주의 국가.

en: braking; a brake or check on something

examples.en: The driver suddenly hit the brakes.

examples.ko: 비 오는 날에는 제동 거리가 길어져요.
examples.en: On rainy days, the braking distance gets longer.

examples.ko: 자전거의 제동이 잘 안 돼서 위험했어요.
examples.en: The bike's brakes didn't work well, so it was dangerous.
The new rule put the brakes on the business.

examples.ko: 정부의 발표로 가격 상승에 제동이 걸렸어요.
examples.en: The government announcement put the brakes on rising prices.
The train stopped because of a problem with the braking system.

explain: 제동은 차나 기계를 멈추게 하는 일을 말해요. 자동차 브레이크를 눌러 속도를 줄일 때 쓰고, 계획이나 흐름을 막는다는 뜻으로도 많이 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '브레이크를 밟다'가 더 흔해요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 차를 멈추는 게 아니라 어떤 일이 더 진행되지 못하게 막을 때 써요. 뉴스에서 자주 들려요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used not for stopping a car but for holding back a trend or plan. Very common in news.

explain_en: 제동 is the act of stopping or slowing a vehicle or machine. It is also used figuratively for stopping a plan or trend. In everyday speech Koreans more often say 브레이크를 밟다 (step on the brake).

examples.en: Everyone hopes for an end to the war.
Experts say the end of the disease is near.
When the declaration of the end came out, people were happy.

examples.ko: 이번 협정은 오랜 갈등의 종식이 될 거예요.
examples.en: This agreement will mark the end of a long conflict.
We gathered for the end of violence.
We still need time before it is over.

explain: 종식은 오래 이어진 나쁜 일이나 큰 문제가 완전히 끝난다는 뜻으로 써요. '끝'이나 '마지막'과 달리, 전쟁·병·갈등처럼 심각한 일에만 주로 써요. '종식을 선언하다', '종식되다'처럼 말해요.
explain_en: 종식 is for a serious, long-running problem finally coming to an end, such as a war, disease or conflict. Unlike plain 끝 (end), it is not used for everyday things like a class or a movie. Common forms are 종식을 선언하다 and 종식되다.

examples.ko: 새 약이 병을 종식시킬 수 있을까요?
examples.en: Can the new medicine bring the disease to an end?
The two countries ended the war through talks.
We have to put an end to this conflict.

examples.ko: 새 법은 오랜 차별을 종식시키려고 만들어졌어요.
examples.en: The new law was made to end long-standing discrimination.
That announcement put the rumors to rest.
The president promised to end the crisis.

explain: '종식시키다'는 누군가가 일부러 어떤 나쁜 상황을 끝내는 거예요. 스스로 끝나는 '종식되다'와 달라요. 전쟁, 갈등, 질병처럼 큰 문제에 써요.
explain_en: 종식시키다 means that someone actively brings a bad situation to an end, unlike 종식되다, which ends by itself. It fits big problems such as war, conflict or disease.

examples.en: This song was made on the spot.
The improvised performance was really cool.
I went on a spur-of-the-moment trip with friends.

examples.ko: 그 배우는 즉흥 연기를 아주 잘해요.
examples.en: That actor is very good at improvised acting.
I gave the presentation off the cuff, so I was really nervous.
Spur-of-the-moment decisions are sometimes regretted.

explain: 즉흥은 미리 준비하지 않고 그 자리에서 바로 하는 거예요. '즉흥 연주', '즉흥 여행'처럼 다른 명사 앞에 붙이거나 '즉흥적이다'로 많이 써요. '계획 없이 갑자기'라는 가볍고 재미있는 느낌이 있을 때가 많아요.
explain_en: 즉흥 means doing something on the spot, with no preparation. It usually sits before another noun, as in 즉흥 연주, or becomes 즉흥적이다. It often has a light, fun feel of acting without a plan.

examples.en: Water evaporates in the hot sun.
All the water in the cup has evaporated.
As sweat evaporates, the body cools down.

examples.ko: 아침 이슬은 해가 뜨면 증발할 거예요.
examples.en: The morning dew will evaporate when the sun comes up.

examples.ko: 한꺼번에 증발하는 물의 양은 생각보다 많아요.
examples.en: The amount of water that evaporates at once is more than you'd think.
As soon as I got paid, my money vanished.

explain: '증발하다'는 액체가 기체로 변해 사라지는 걸 말해요. 요즘 구어에서는 돈이나 사람이 갑자기 어디론가 없어졌을 때 농담처럼도 써요. '끓다'는 열을 받아 보글보글하는 것이라서 증발과는 달라요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 물이 아니라 돈이나 사람이 흔적 없이 사라질 때 쓰는 비유예요.
phrases.nuance_en: A figurative use for money or people that vanish without a trace.

explain_en: 증발하다 describes a liquid turning into gas and disappearing. In casual speech it is also used jokingly when money or a person suddenly vanishes. It differs from 끓다 (to boil), which is about bubbling under heat.

en: birth; origin (place or background one is born into)

examples.en: That singer was born in Busan.

examples.ko: 서울 태생인 친구가 사투리를 못 알아들어요.
examples.en: My friend, a Seoul native, can't understand the dialect.

examples.ko: 그는 가난한 집안 태생이지만 열심히 일했어요.
examples.en: Though born into a poor family, they worked hard.
I was born abroad, so my Korean is clumsy.
Though our backgrounds differ, we are good friends.
He was born in the countryside, so he likes nature.

explain: 태생은 어디에서, 어떤 집안에서 태어났는지를 말해요. '서울 태생'처럼 '지역 + 태생'으로 가장 많이 써요. 같은 뜻으로 '출신'이 있는데, 출신은 태어난 곳뿐 아니라 졸업한 학교나 직장에도 써요.
explain_en: 태생 tells where or into what family someone was born, most often in the pattern place + 태생, like 서울 태생. 출신 is a close word, but it also covers schools and workplaces one came from, not just birth.

examples.en: The road was flooded from a burst water pipe.
The hospital said it was a ruptured eardrum.
There was an accident caused by a tire blowout.
A ruptured blood vessel is very dangerous.

examples.ko: 배관이 오래되면 파열이 일어날 수 있어요.
examples.en: If pipes get old, they can burst.
A gas pipe rupture occurred during construction.

explain: 파열은 물건이나 몸 안의 무언가가 압력 때문에 터져서 찢어지는 거예요. 수도관, 혈관, 고막, 타이어에 자주 써요. 불이나 큰 소리가 나는 '폭발'과는 달라서 터진 부분이 갈라지거나 새어 나오는 느낌이에요.
explain_en: 파열 is when something under pressure splits open, such as a water pipe, blood vessel, eardrum or tire. It differs from 폭발 (explosion): the focus is on a tear or leak, not a blast.

examples.en: The president arrived under police escort.

examples.ko: 배는 군함의 호위 속에 항구를 떠났어요.
examples.en: The ship left port under the escort of a warship.

examples.ko: 왕을 호위하는 병사가 문 앞에 서 있어요.
examples.en: The soldiers guarding the king stand at the door.
Escort vehicles follow in front and behind.
In the movie, the bodyguard warrior protected the hero.
Without an escort, this road is dangerous.

explain: 호위는 중요한 사람이나 물건을 따라다니며 지키는 일이에요. 경호는 주로 사람을 지키는 일에 쓰고, 호위는 함께 움직이며 둘러싸 지키는 모습에 더 잘 어울려요. 옛날 이야기와 군대, 뉴스에서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: 호위 means accompanying an important person or thing in order to protect it. 경호 is more about guarding a person; 호위 fits protection while moving together. It shows up in historical stories, the military and the news.

examples.en: Police cars escort the president's car.
Warships escorted the merchant ships.
The soldiers walked while guarding the king.

examples.ko: 공연 내내 경호원이 가수를 호위할 거예요.
examples.en: Bodyguards will escort the singer throughout the concert.
Nobody escorts me.

examples.ko: 어린 사자를 호위하는 어른 사자들이 있어요.
examples.en: There are adult lions that guard the young lion.

explain: '호위하다'는 중요한 사람이나 배, 차를 따라가면서 지키는 거예요. '지키다'보다 격식 있고, 움직이는 대상 옆에서 함께 간다는 느낌이 강해요. 보통 '~을/를 호위하다' 모양으로 써요.
explain_en: 호위하다 means to protect something important while travelling with it, such as a person, ship or vehicle. It is more formal than 지키다, with a strong sense of moving alongside. The usual pattern is ~을/를 호위하다.

examples.en: Certificates are issued at the counter.
It takes about a week to issue an ID card.
I applied to have the document issued at the community center.
Diplomas are handed out at the graduation ceremony.
The issuing fee is one thousand won.

examples.ko: 허가증 교부가 늦어져서 일을 시작하지 못했어요.
examples.en: The permit was delayed, so I couldn't start work.

explain: 교부는 관청이나 학교 같은 곳에서 증명서나 허가증 같은 공식 서류를 내주는 일이에요. 일반적으로 물건을 주는 '주다'와 달리 서류를 정식으로 내줄 때만 써요. '발급'과 비슷한데, 발급은 서류를 만들어 내는 쪽에, 교부는 건네주는 쪽에 초점이 있어요.
explain_en: 교부 is the official handing over of documents such as certificates and permits by an office or school. Unlike plain 주다 (give), it is used only for formal paperwork. 발급 is close, but it focuses on producing the document, while 교부 focuses on handing it over.

examples.en: City Hall issues certificates.
The school handed diplomas to the graduates.
They will issue the permit tomorrow morning.
You need an ID to have the documents issued.
The staff member handed over the receipt and then said goodbye.
The documents handed out at the counter are free.

explain: '교부하다'는 관청이나 학교가 공식 서류를 사람에게 내주는 거예요. 같은 뜻으로 '발급하다'를 더 많이 쓰고, 교부하다는 조금 딱딱한 서류 느낌이에요. 일상에서 서류를 받을 때는 '받다'라고 하면 돼요.
explain_en: 교부하다 is when an office or school officially hands a document to someone. 발급하다 is more common, and 교부하다 sounds more bureaucratic. As the receiver in daily life, simply say 받다.

examples.en: The city is growing rapidly.
Technological progress is really rapid.
It is hard to adapt to rapid change.
The disease spread quickly.
Internet speeds have gotten rapidly faster these days.
The ice is melting rapidly.

explain: '급속하다'는 변화나 진행이 아주 빠르게 일어날 때 써요. '빠르다'는 속도 자체를 말하고, 급속하다는 성장·확산·변화처럼 흐름에 주로 써요. 보통 '급속히', '급속하게', '급속한 ~' 형태로 나와요.
explain_en: 급속하다 describes a change or process that happens very quickly. 빠르다 describes speed in general, while 급속하다 is for growth, spread or change. It usually appears as 급속히, 급속하게 or 급속한 + noun.

en: old and worn out; aged (of buildings, equipment)

examples.en: This building has become very worn out.
We need to replace the aged water pipes.

examples.ko: 우리 아파트는 너무 노후해서 비가 새요.
examples.en: Our apartment is so old that it leaks when it rains.
If school facilities are worn out, safety is a concern.

examples.ko: 노후하다는 이유로 다리를 새로 짓기로 했어요.
examples.en: They decided to rebuild the bridge because it is aging.

examples.ko: 노후한 기계 때문에 공장이 자주 멈춰요.
examples.en: The factory often stops because of its worn-out machines.

explain: '노후하다'는 건물, 다리, 기계처럼 오래 써서 낡고 약해졌다는 뜻이에요. 물건이나 시설에만 쓰고 사람에게는 쓰지 않아요. 사람이 나이 들 때는 '늙다'를 쓰고, 일반 물건이 낡을 때는 '낡다'가 훨씬 자주 나와요.
explain_en: 노후하다 is only for things such as buildings, bridges and machines that have grown old and weak through long use, never for people. For people, use 늙다. For ordinary worn items, 낡다 is much more common.

en: be humiliated; be disgraced; lose face in public

examples.en: I was greatly humiliated in front of everyone.
I got embarrassed at the interview because I got the name wrong.
If you do that, you will lose face.
I was shamed in front of my friends, and my face turned red.
I prepared hard so I wouldn't be humiliated.

examples.ko: 시험에서 꼴찌를 해서 망신당할까 봐 걱정돼요.
examples.en: I'm afraid I'll be humiliated by coming in last on the test.

explain: '망신당하다'는 다른 사람들 앞에서 실수하거나 잘못이 드러나서 체면을 잃는 거예요. 내 잘못이든 아니든 남이 보는 곳에서 창피한 일을 겪는다는 느낌이에요. '창피하다'는 부끄러운 마음 자체이고, 망신당하다는 그런 일을 겪는 상황이에요.
explain_en: 망신당하다 means losing face when a mistake or fault is exposed in front of others. 창피하다 is the feeling of embarrassment itself, while 망신당하다 is the situation of going through it publicly.

examples.en: When I think of that, it still feels shameful.
Getting such an easy question wrong is embarrassing.
I'm sorry for showing such an embarrassing side of me.

examples.ko: 친구들 앞에서 우는 건 망신스러운 일이 아니에요.
examples.en: Crying in front of friends is nothing to be ashamed of.
After boasting so loudly, losing is shameful.
I was so ashamed that I couldn't lift my head.

explain: '망신스럽다'는 남 앞에서 체면이 깎이는 일이라서 느껴지는 창피함이에요. '부끄럽다'는 마음속에서 느끼는 감정이 많고, 망신스럽다는 다른 사람의 시선이 중요해요. 어떤 상황이 보기에 부끄러울 때도 써요.
explain_en: 망신스럽다 is shame tied to losing face in front of others. 부끄럽다 is more of an inner feeling, whereas 망신스럽다 puts weight on how others see you. It can also describe a situation that looks shameful.

examples.en: The child embarrassed their dad in front of the guests.
You shouldn't embarrass a friend on purpose.
Did you do that to embarrass me?
That person humiliated a team member in the meeting.
Don't do anything that shames your family.
If you're thinking of embarrassing me, stop.

explain: '망신시키다'는 일부러든 아니든 누군가를 남 앞에서 창피하게 만드는 거예요. 내가 스스로 망신을 겪는 '망신당하다'와 짝이에요. '가문을 망신시키다'처럼 가족이나 집단의 명예를 해칠 때도 써요.
explain_en: 망신시키다 means making someone look bad in front of others, intentionally or not. It pairs with 망신당하다, where the person themselves goes through the shame. It is also used when someone damages the honor of a family or group.

examples.en: I was put to shame, and my face turned red.
I made an embarrassed face at the teacher's words.
I didn't say it to embarrass you.
I was too embarrassed to say anything.
That person laughed to hide their embarrassment.
Before my embarrassment even faded, I made another mistake.

explain: 무안은 남 앞에서 어색하고 부끄러운 마음이에요. 말을 잘못했거나 무시당했을 때 얼굴이 달아오르는 느낌과 가까워요. 보통 '무안을 주다', '무안을 당하다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: 무안 is an awkward, ashamed feeling in front of others, like when you say the wrong thing or feel slighted and your face goes warm. It is commonly used as 무안을 주다 (to embarrass someone) and 무안을 당하다 (to be embarrassed).

examples.en: I felt embarrassed when my name was called out loudly.

examples.ko: 혼자 아무 말도 못 하니까 좀 무안해요.
examples.en: It's a bit awkward that I can't say anything.
Feeling awkward, I left the spot quickly.
When my gift was turned down, I got embarrassed and blushed.
I pretended not to notice so they wouldn't feel awkward.

examples.ko: 그렇게 말하면 상대가 무안할 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you say it like that, the other person might feel awkward.

explain: '무안하다'는 남 앞에서 어색하고 쑥스럽다는 뜻이에요. '부끄럽다'보다 상대방과의 관계에서 오는 어색함에 가까워요. 상대가 민망할까 봐 '무안하지 않게 해 주다'처럼 배려의 말로도 많이 써요.
explain_en: 무안하다 is feeling awkward or sheepish around others. It is closer to social awkwardness between people than 부끄럽다. A common considerate phrase is 무안하지 않게 해 주다 (to spare someone the awkwardness).

en: spur (on a riding boot); extra push

examples.en: The jockey's boots have spurs on them.
We stepped up the construction and finished early.
We are speeding up the development of the new product.
The exam was coming, so I picked up the pace of studying.

examples.ko: 계약 소식에 팀이 준비에 박차를 가했어요.
examples.en: After the news of the contract, the team stepped up its preparations.
You shouldn't use spurs on a horse.

explain: 박차는 원래 말을 탈 때 신발 뒤꿈치에 다는 뾰족한 도구예요. 하지만 일상에서는 거의 '박차를 가하다' 한 가지로 써요. 하던 일을 더 빠르고 힘차게 밀어붙일 때 말해요.

phrases.example: 정부가 일자리 만들기에 박차를 가하고 있어요.
phrases.nuance_ko: 이미 하고 있는 일에 속도와 힘을 더 낼 때 써요. 새로 시작할 때는 쓰지 않아요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used for adding speed and effort to something already underway, not for starting something new.

explain_en: 박차 is originally the spur on a rider's boot heel. In everyday Korean it appears almost only in the phrase 박차를 가하다, meaning to speed up and push ahead with something one is already doing.

examples.en: Angry, they kicked the door open.
The athlete kicked off the ground and jumped high.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 안정된 직장을 박차고 나왔어요.
examples.en: That person walked out on a stable job.
You have to throw off the blanket and get up.
If you kick the ball hard, it flies far.

examples.ko: 자유를 위해 모든 걸 박차고 떠났어요.
examples.en: They threw everything aside and left for freedom.

explain: '박차다'는 발로 세게 차거나 힘차게 밀어내는 거예요. 그냥 '차다'보다 힘과 결단이 느껴져요. '문을 박차고 나가다', '이불을 박차고 일어나다'처럼 어떤 상황을 확 뿌리치고 나갈 때 비유로도 써요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 참거나 머물던 곳을 확 뿌리치고 떠날 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used for leaving a place or situation abruptly and decisively.

explain_en: 박차다 means to kick or push off with strong force, with more power and resolve than plain 차다 (to kick). It is also used figuratively for breaking away, as in 문을 박차고 나가다 (storm out) and 이불을 박차고 일어나다 (throw off the covers and get up).

en: detailed; minute; thorough (down to small points)

examples.en: The teacher explained it in fine detail.
The plan is detailed, so it's easy to follow.
Please check even the small details.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 모든 걸 세세히 기억해요.
examples.en: That person remembers everything in detail.

examples.ko: 안내서가 너무 세세해서 오히려 읽기 힘들어요.
examples.en: The guide is so detailed that it's hard to read.
I was grateful for my mother's careful attention to detail.

explain: '세세하다'는 작은 부분까지 꼼꼼하고 자세하다는 뜻이에요. '자세하다'와 비슷하지만 세세하다는 작은 항목을 하나하나 짚는 느낌이 더 강해요. 보통 '세세하게', '세세히'로 많이 말해요.
explain_en: 세세하다 means attending to small points one by one. It is close to 자세하다, but with a stronger feeling of going through each little item. You mostly hear it as 세세하게 or 세세히.
